blocks.x: Core definitions
Chemical bond The force of attraction between two atoms; bonds form to achieve a more stable outer electronic configuration — the doublet or octet rule.
Ionic bond Formed by the complete transfer of electrons between atoms; the resulting bond is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions.
Covalent bond Formed by the sharing of electrons between atoms; occurs as a sigma (σ) or pi (π) bond.
Hybridization The mutual mixing of atomic orbitals of different shapes and energies to form new orbitals of equal energy, shape and direction.

Atom→ Bond formed
(ionic / covalent / coordinate)→ Hybridized orbitals→ Molecular shape→ Polarity→ Physical & biological properties
Hybridization, shape & bond angle at a glance
NH₃ (107°) and H₂O (104.5°) are both sp³ but their tetrahedral angle is compressed by 1 and 2 lone pairs respectively — a "distorted tetrahedron".
Ionic · Covalent · Coordinate

Atoms transfer or share electrons to reach a more stable outer electronic configuration. Three mechanisms of bond formation were covered: ionic, covalent (sigma and pi), and coordinate (dative) covalent bonding.
Ionic (electrovalent) bond
Formed by the complete transfer of electrons between the atoms that form the compound:

Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl
The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions constitutes the ionic bond. Read further: Born-Haber Cycle and Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation.

blocks.title: Factors that favour ionic bond formation

blocks.x: Note: for the EN difference, the value should be ≥ 1.7 for a bond to be considered ionic.
Electronegativity difference decides the bond type
Covalent bond
Formed by the sharing of electrons between atoms:

H· + H· → H:H → H₂ = H–H
O: + :O → O:O → O₂ = O=O
There are two types of covalent bonds: sigma (σ) and pi (π).
An end-to-end / head-on overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear line (s–s, s–p or p–p overlap). Example: in ethane (C₂H₆), the C–C bond and all C–H bonds are sigma bonds.

A side-to-side / lateral overlap of atomic orbitals away from the internuclear axis. Example: ethene (C₂H₄) has one pi bond. Pi bonds are weaker and more reactive — easily broken to make electrons available for reaction.

blocks.title: Sigma vs. pi bond — full comparison

c: Overlapping orbitals can be pure or hybrid
Must exist along with a sigma bond
Has an impact on the shape of molecules
Has no role in determining molecular shape

blocks.x: Coordinate (dative) covalent bond
The shared electron pair is donated by one of the bonded atoms. Examples: NH₄⁺ (N donates a lone pair to H⁺) and H₃O⁺ (O donates a lone pair to a proton).

BF₃ + NH₃ → H₃N–BF₃ — the donor N atom in NH₃ (the Lewis base) donates a lone pair; the acceptor B atom in BF₃ (the Lewis acid) has an empty orbital to accept it, forming a Lewis adduct held together by a coordinate bond.

Haemoglobin & the haem group Some essential organic molecules of the body contain coordinate covalent bonds. In haemoglobin, the haem group has an Fe²⁺ ion that forms a dative covalent bond with the nitrogen atoms of the four pyrrole rings.
Orbitals · Angles · Geometry

Hybridization is the mutual mixing of atomic orbitals of different shapes and energies to form orbitals of equal energy, shape and direction — and it is what sets a molecule's bond angle and 3D shape.
Ground state vs. excited state

In methane (CH₄), carbon's ground state (2s²2p²) has only 2 unpaired electrons, suggesting it should be divalent. But one of the 2s electrons is promoted to the empty 2p orbital, giving the excited state 2s&sup9;2p³ (4 unpaired electrons) — making carbon tetravalent.
Hybridization types & example molecules
sp³, sp² and sp hybridization
sp³ — Methane 109°
4 orbitals involved. Shape: tetrahedral. All 4 orbitals are hybridized; no unhybridized orbital remains.
sp² — Ethene 120°
3 orbitals hybridized (trigonal shape); 1 orbital left unhybridized — this one forms the pi bond.
sp — Ethyne 180°
2 orbitals hybridized (linear shape); 2 orbitals left unhybridized — these form the two pi bonds of the triple bond.
Multiple bonds & hybridization
In compound formation, atoms transfer or share electrons to attain a noble gas configuration (e.g. Na⁺Cl⁻ → NaCl, giving {Ne, Ar} configurations).
Double bond — one sigma + one pi bond — sp² hybridization Triple bond — one sigma + two pi bonds — sp hybridization

blocks.title: Exceptions to the octet rule: expanded & deficient octets

blocks.x: The octet rule holds for period 2 elements such as C, N, O and F, but fails for elements in which d-orbitals are available.

items: Expanded octet — e.g. PCl₅, whose central atom's valence shell holds more than 8 electrons.
Deficient octet — e.g. BF₃, whose central atom's valence shell holds fewer than 8 electrons.

blocks.x: Whether expanded or deficient, neither configuration obeys the octet rule.
Lone pairs, bonded pairs & VSEPR
A lone pair provides a region of greater electron density than a bonded pair, whose density is spread between the bonded atoms. This gives an order of decreasing repulsion:
Lone pair : Lone pair > Lone pair : Bonded pair > Bonded pair : Bonded pair
VSEPR theory Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory states that the arrangement of electron pairs should minimise repulsion to ensure the stability of molecules.
Bond angles: CH₄ vs. NH₃ vs. H₂O
NH₃ and H₂O are both described as a "distorted tetrahedron" — each extra lone pair increases repulsion on the bonded pairs, compressing the angle further below the ideal 109°.
Shape governs molecular behaviour

The shape of a molecule is a significant property because it affects the molecule's behaviour — the shapes of many organic molecules determine their odour, reactivity, taste, and in some cases their action as drugs.

Enzyme–substrate interaction depends on shape: the "lock and key" hypothesis supposes the enzyme is a lock with a specific shape, so it has only a complementary substrate (key) — giving catalysis its specificity.
Dipoles · Van der Waals · Hydrogen bonding

Whether a covalent molecule is polar depends on electronegativity difference and molecular shape. Weaker intermolecular forces — van der Waals and hydrogen bonding — then shape a compound's physical (not chemical) properties.
Polar vs. nonpolar
Made of similar atoms — no tendency for one atom to attract the shared electrons more. Examples: H₂, Cl₂, O₂.
Made of different atoms — one atom attracts the shared electrons more. Example: Hδ+–Clδ−.
The greater the EN difference, the more polar the bond. Decreasing order of polarity for the hydrogen halides: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
What determines a molecule's polarity?
Electronegativity difference
A larger EN difference between bonded atoms gives a more polar bond.
Shape of the molecule
Even with polar bonds, a symmetric shape can cancel out the individual bond dipoles.
EXAMPLE: CARBON DIOXIDE
O = C = O

Both C=O bonds are individually polar, but CO₂'s linear shape places them in exactly opposite directions — since both sides are polar in opposing directions, it cancels out, so the molecule as a whole has no net polarity.
Intramolecular vs. intermolecular forces

Ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds are intramolecular forces. Intermolecular forces can account for differences in the physical state of molecules: CH₄ and H₂S are gases, H₂O and CHCl₃ (chloroform) are liquids, and C₆H₅COOH (benzoic acid) is a solid.

Temporary induced dipole–induced dipole attraction, very predominant in non-polar molecules. Distortion of the electron cloud creates a temporary dipole that induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule.
Larger molecular size → more electrons → greater electron-cloud distortion → stronger van der Waals forces. Example: F₂, Cl₂ (gases) < Br₂ (liquid) < I₂ (solid).
A unique permanent dipole–dipole attraction between hydrogen and N, O, or F. Not a covalent bond to a hydrogen atom.
Why HF and H₂O don't behave like their neighbours

Boiling points of hydrogen halides increase: HCl < HBr < HI < HF. Hydrogen bonding is strongly possible in HF, slightly possible in HCl, and non-existent in HBr and HI. The strong hydrogen bonding in HF gives its molecules an associated, liquid nature — unlike the other, gaseous, hydrogen halides. Likewise, H₂O is liquid while H₂S and H₂Se are gases, because water molecules become associated through hydrogen bonding.

blocks.title: Effect of hydrogen bonding on solubility

blocks.x: "Like dissolves like." Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents but not nonpolar ones.

items: NaCl dissolves in water (attraction between Na⁺/Cl⁻ and polar water > attraction between the ions themselves) but not in ether (a nonpolar solvent cannot attract the ions).

Candle wax does not dissolve in water (strong hydrogen bonding in water prevents interaction with the hydrocarbon wax), but the wax does dissolve in petrol, since the van der Waals attraction between wax and petrol is greater than that between the solute wax particles.

blocks.title: Other effects of hydrogen bonding in biology

items: Makes the helical structure of DNA possible; because these bonds are weak, the two strands can unwind — an essential step in DNA replication.
A higher degree of hydrogen bonding among the straight-chain glucose polymers of cellulose makes it more rigid than starch or glycogen, which have a lower degree of hydrogen bonding.

blocks.x: Physical, not chemical, properties Because intermolecular forces are far weaker than intramolecular (bonding) forces, they do not directly affect a compound's chemical properties — only its physical properties: physical state, solubility, boiling point, melting point, specific heat, molar heat of fusion/vaporization, viscosity, and surface tension.
Same formula, different connectivity
Isomerism is a phenomenon where different structures (isomers) can represent compounds of the same molecular formula. Structural isomers differ in the way their constituent atoms are connected.
Isomerism at a glance

Isomerism→ Structural
(chain / positional / functional / tautomerism) Stereoisomerism
(conformational / configurational)
Isomers differ in the chain type.
Butane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ (straight chain) 2-methylpropane CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃ (branched chain)
Both are C₄H₁₀.
Isomers differ in the placement of the functional group.
Propan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂OH Propan-2-ol CH₃CH(OH)CH₃
Both are C₃H₄OH.
Isomers differ in the functional group itself.
Dimethyl ether CH₃–O–CH₃ Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH
Both are C₂H₆O.
Functional groups in dynamic equilibrium; tautomers are mutually interconvertible.
Keto (2-propanone) ~99.9% stable Enol (propen-2-ol) ~0.001% stable
Both are C₃H₆O.
Same connectivity, different 3D arrangement

Stereoisomers share identical atom connectivity but differ in the arrangement of atoms in three-dimensional space. This lecture covers conformational stereoisomerism, and configurational stereoisomerism (geometric and optical).
Conformational stereoisomerism
Arises from the possibility of free rotation about a C–C single covalent bond. The individual structures are called conformers: staggered and eclipsed conformers (example: C₂H₃Cl₃).
Geometric isomerism
Due to hindered rotation about a C=C double bond or a ring system. The attached groups on the double-bonded carbon(s) must be different.
cis-2-butene less stable
The two CH₃ groups sit on the same side of the C=C bond.
trans-2-butene more stable
The bulky CH₃ groups are wide apart across the C=C bond, giving minimum repulsion.
Maleic acid cis-butenedioic acid
The less stable cis form of butenedioic acid.
Fumaric acid trans-butenedioic acid
The more stable trans form — minimum steric repulsion.
Ring compounds can also cause geometric isomerism by making a molecule rigid, e.g. cis/trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane.
Used when 3 or 4 different groups are attached to a C=C bond. E represents across, and Z represents together.
Priorities are assigned by atomic number — the higher the atomic number, the higher the priority: F < Cl < Br < I (increasing priority). Alphabetical order is also considered when naming.
Example: the compound with Br & I on one carbon and Cl & F on the other is named E-1-bromo-2-chloro-2-fluoro-1-iodoethene.
Optical isomerism
Molecules interact differently with plane-polarised light (ppl). Those that interact are optically active — rotating the light either right (dextro-rotatory) or left (laevo-rotatory).
Chiral optically active
A tetrahedral (sp³) carbon bonded to four different groups.
Achiral optically inactive
Bonded to at least two similar groups.
Enantiomers & diastereoisomers

Enantiomers Non-superimposable mirror images of each other. Example: L(+) and D(−) lactic acid. They share identical physical properties except for the direction of ppl rotation, identical chemical properties with optically inactive reagents (but different with optically active ones), and different physiological properties — e.g. (−)-nicotine is more poisonous than (+)-nicotine.

Diastereoisomers Stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other. Example (2,3-dihydroxybutanoic acid): A & B are enantiomers, C & D are enantiomers — but A & C (or A & D) are diastereoisomers. The number of possible isomers = 2n, where n is the number of chiral (asymmetric) carbon centres.

Meso compounds In tartaric acid (2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid), E and F are enantiomers, while E (or F) and G are diastereoisomers. G is mesotartaric acid — optically inactive despite having chiral centres, because the rotation from the lower half cancels the rotation from the upper half.
Racemic mixture & resolution

A racemic mixture is an equimolar mixture of two enantiomers, e.g. (+/−) lactic acid. It is optically inactive because the laevo rotation is cancelled by an equal but opposite dextro rotation. Separating a racemic mixture is called resolution.

blocks.title: Three ways to resolve a racemic mixture

items: Biological system: e.g. Penicillium glaucum media consumes the (+) lactic acid but not the (−) form.
Affinity chromatography: a ligand attached to the column support binds selectively to one enantiomer.

Diastereomer formation: the racemic mixture is combined with an optically active compound, forming diastereoisomers that can be separated by fractional crystallisation based on differences in solubility.

blocks.x: What gives a molecule its personality
Atoms or groups of atoms that, when present in organic compounds, determine the compound's physical and chemical properties.

Example: ethane (CH₃CH₃) is an unreactive gas. Remove an H and add –COOH: you get propionic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH). Remove an H and add –OH: you get ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH). Both resulting compounds are soluble in water and far more reactive than ethane.
